summary: Compares ways of providing keys to protect RSVP messages hop by hop: one key for a group, or separate keys per neighbor or interface. It looks at how keys get provisioned and where each approach works or falls short, and also considers encrypting RSVP messages. This is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers that pass notes to each other can lock them with a secret code. This compares sharing one code with everybody against giving each pair of neighbors its own, and how to hand out the codes.

subtitle: Comparing methods to protect router-to-router messages in quality-of-service networks.

tldr.problem: RSVP routers authenticate each other using shared secrets, but deciding how to distribute and manage those secrets is operationally difficult. A network can use one key for everyone, one key per neighboring pair, or something in between.
tldr.mechanism: The document compares three approaches: per-neighbor keys (high security but hard to manage), group keys (shared across many routers, easier to manage), and the use of IPsec or other encryption methods, explaining where each works well and where it falls short.
tldr.outcome: Network operators can choose the keying method that fits their deployment: group keys for a single trusted domain, per-neighbor keys between security domains, and group keys for scenarios with non-RSVP hops.

today: RFC 6411 is an Informational document that provides guidance to network operators deploying RSVP. It has not been obsoleted and remains the reference for understanding the trade-offs between different RSVP keying strategies.

sections.title: The Problem of Key Management
sections.content:
The Resource Reservation Protocol (RSVP) allows routers to reserve bandwidth and set up paths for multimedia traffic. To prevent spoofing and tampering, RSVP messages are authenticated using an integrity object containing a keyed message digest. However, RFC 2747 does not specify how the key should be derived or distributed.

In practice, most RSVP deployments use a static key that is manually configured. The difficulty is that changing keys across a large network requires careful coordination to avoid breaking RSVP operation. Many operators resort to using the same key throughout their entire RSVP network and change it rarely, if ever, creating a security risk. This document explores different keying strategies and when each is appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers that use RSVP to manage traffic need secret codes to check that messages are real. But deciding how to hand out and change those codes is hard, and many networks just use one code everywhere.

sections.title: The Hop-by-Hop Trust Model
sections.content:
RSVP operates on a hop-by-hop authentication model where each router trusts only its immediate neighbors through a shared key. Trust is transitive: if router A trusts router B and router B trusts router C, then A implicitly trusts C. When a per-neighbor key is used, each router pair shares a unique key. When a group key is used, all members of a security domain share the same key, and authentication is based on group membership rather than individual peer identity.

A complication arises when non-RSVP routers exist on the path between RSVP speakers. Because RSVP routers do not always know which RSVP neighbor will process their message (especially with dynamic routing), they cannot easily use per-neighbor keys. Group keys work naturally in this case, since the message is protected regardless of which RSVP router receives it next.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router checks the code on messages from its neighbors. If everybody in one building has the same code, that's easier but less secure than each pair having their own code. When messages skip over non-RSVP routers, the group code works better.

sections.title: Per-Neighbor Keys versus Group Keys
sections.content:
Per-neighbor and per-interface keys provide fine-grained security: each RSVP speaker shares a different key with each neighbor or interface. This is ideal within a single security domain where all routers trust each other. The tradeoff is operational complexity: provisioning and rotating individual keys across many routers is labor-intensive. Per-neighbor keys work well between security domains where different operators control the routers.

Group keys simplify management by having all members of a security domain use the same key. A Group Key Server (GKS) administers membership and distributes keys. Group keys are naturally suited to intra-domain deployments where all routers belong to the same trusted domain. They also handle non-RSVP hops gracefully. A single group key cannot easily span multiple security domains unless a single key server is trusted by all domains, which is rare in practice. A better multi-domain approach is to use separate group keys within each domain and per-neighbor keys between domains.
sections.plainLanguage: Each pair of neighbors can have their own secret code for maximum security, but that means setting up and changing a lot of codes. Or everybody in one building can share one code, which is easier but means anyone in that building can spoof messages. Non-RSVP routers in the path make shared codes better.

sections.title: Static and Dynamic Key Provisioning
sections.content:
Static key provisioning means preconfiguring keys manually or through a network management system. This is the simplest approach but does not scale well. Synchronizing a key change across an entire network is difficult: if you change the key at different times on different routers, RSVP operation will suffer. A grace period is needed during which both old and new keys are accepted.

Dynamic keying methods automatically negotiate or distribute keys without manual intervention. Per-neighbor dynamic keying can use protocols like IKE to negotiate unique keys between adjacent routers. Dynamic group key distribution can use GDOI (Group Domain of Interpretation) or similar protocols: each router requests a group key from the key server using an encrypted and integrity-protected handshake, avoiding the need for static provisioning while still leveraging public key mechanisms for authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: You can set up codes by hand (simple but tedious), or have the routers automatically agree on codes when they connect (more work to set up, but easier to change later).

sections.title: When to Use Group Keying
sections.content:
Several RSVP deployment scenarios especially benefit from group keying. RSVP Notify messages, which are sent non-hop-by-hop in some cases (for example, directly from an ingress node to an egress node in MPLS traffic engineering), are difficult to protect with per-neighbor keys but work well with group keys. RSVP-TE Fast Reroute scenarios may cause a Point of Local Repair (PLR) and a Merge Point to become RSVP neighbors during a failure recovery without prior configuration; group keying avoids the need to provision keys for every possible pair.

GMPLS LSP Hierarchy and Point-to-Multipoint RSVP-TE both use non-hop-by-hop signaling and can simplify security by using group keying. In all these cases, the advantage of group keying is that it eliminates the need for pre-provisioned per-neighbor keys while still maintaining hop-by-hop authentication semantics.
sections.plainLanguage: Some special cases in RSVP don't know ahead of time which routers will need to talk to each other. Group codes solve this because any router in the group can verify a message.

sections.title: IPsec as an Alternative
sections.content:
IPsec can be used to protect RSVP messages at the IP layer, providing integrity and optionally encryption. The document notes that IPsec has some advantages and tradeoffs compared to RSVP's built-in INTEGRITY object. IPsec tunnel mode can provide protection for the entire IP header and contents, whereas the INTEGRITY object protects only the RSVP message itself. However, IPsec tunnel mode does not work well in the presence of non-RSVP hops because a router does not know the next RSVP hop address.

Tunnel mode with address preservation, defined in RFC 5374, addresses this limitation by copying addresses from the inner header to the outer header. This mode allows IPsec to be used with group keying even when non-RSVP routers are on the path. The keying methods discussed earlier (per-neighbor, group, static, dynamic) apply equally whether protecting RSVP with the INTEGRITY object or with IPsec.
sections.plainLanguage: The IP layer itself can lock messages, which protects more information but doesn't work when non-RSVP routers are in the way, unless you use a special mode that preserves addresses.
